titles: Patron of Commerce and Worldly Prosperity
Guardian of the Harvest and Sustenance
canonical_lore: Inari Ōkami (稲荷大神) is the kami of rice, agriculture, sake, and—by extension—of commerce and worldly prosperity, and is among the most widely worshipped deities in Japan, enshrined at roughly 30,000 Inari shrines nationwide. The name is a collective one: at its core stands Uka-no-Mitama-no-Kami (宇迦之御魂神), the 'spirit of the grain,' who appears in the Kojiki (古事記) as a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto (須佐之男命) and in the Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) as a child of Izanagi and Izanami. From the Heian period the deity's cult broadened from rice and the harvest to general prosperity, and through Buddhist syncretism (honji-suijaku) Inari became identified with the goddess Dakiniten (荼枳尼天). The fox (kitsune, 狐) is revered as Inari's messenger (tsukai, 使い)—not the deity itself—and pairs of stone foxes, often holding a key or a sheaf of rice in their mouths, guard Inari shrines. The head shrine of the cult is Fushimi Inari Taisha (伏見稲荷大社) in Kyoto, founded in 711 CE.
